## Introduction

### Overview

Since [week 12](/week12/w12b_r-basics.qmd#quarto-documents),
you've been writing your R code in Quarto documents,
using a basic YAML header, code chunks, and Markdown text.
In this session, we'll take a closer look at each of these components,
and at what happens when you render a document.
We'll also see how to record the R and package versions you used.

### Learning goals

In this session, you will learn:

-   What happens when Quarto renders a document
-   More about **YAML** syntax and useful options in the YAML header
-   How to use **chunk options**, including for figures, and how to set them for a whole document
-   How to include R output in your Markdown text
-   How to record the versions of R and R packages that you used
-   How to render a document to Markdown that displays well on GitHub

### Setting up

- Create a new folder `week14` in your personal dir,
  and [open it in Positron](/week12/w12b_r-basics.qmd#working-directory-and-opening-a-folder).
- Create a new Quarto document `week14/week14a.qmd` and open it.

## Rendering Quarto documents

### How rendering works

When you render a Quarto document, a two-step process occurs:

1. **All code is run** by *knitr* to produce a plain Markdown file with your text,
   code, and the code's output.
2. The Markdown file is then **converted** to the final output format by *Pandoc*.

This two-step process means that the same `.qmd` file can be rendered to many output formats,
like HTML, PDF, Word, and even slide decks and websites^[
This website and its slides were made with Quarto, too!],
and that Quarto isn't limited to R:
it can also run code in other languages like Python.

### Rendering from the terminal

You can also render a Quarto document from the terminal,
using the `quarto render` command:

```bash
quarto render week14a.qmd
```

This is similar to the "Preview" button in Positron,
but it does a **one-time render** and does not show the result in the Viewer pane.

It's a good idea to include this command in your project's **protocol** or README file:
that is clearer and more reproducible than notes about which Quarto document
to open and which button to click.

## The YAML header revisited

The YAML header contains settings for the document:
metadata like the title and author, and options for the output format.
Recall from week 12 that each line contains a `key: value` pair (with a space after the colon).
Here is an example with a few more options
(for more, see [these Quarto docs {{< fa external-link >}}](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-basics.html){target="_blank"}):

```yaml
---
title: "Week 14: Quarto"
subtitle: "Beyond the basics"
author: "Jane Doe"
date: 2026-11-23
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    theme: cosmo
    embed-resources: true
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
---
```

- Keys can be **nested** by indenting them with two spaces:
  above, `html` is nested under `format`, and `toc` is nested under `html`.
- `toc: true` adds a **table of contents**.
- `theme` picks one of Quarto's
  [25 built-in **themes** {{< fa external-link >}}](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-themes.html){target="_blank"},
  which change the fonts, colors, etc.
- `embed-resources: true` makes Quarto put everything,
  including any figures, into a single HTML file,
  so you can download that one file from OSC and open or share it^[
    When you don't embed resources, Quarto creates a separate folder with the figures.
  ].
- `execute:` sets **default options for all code chunks** in the document.
  Above, `echo: false` hides all R code by default (showing only the output),
  and `warning: false` hides warnings.
  Note that `execute:` is a top-level key, not nested under `format:`.
  Below, you'll see how to override these defaults for individual chunks.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Want to show your rendered output on GitHub? _(Click to expand)_

GitHub shows HTML files as raw code, not as web pages.
To share a rendered document in a GitHub repository, like for your final project,
you can _also_ render it to GitHub-Flavored Markdown (`gfm`), which GitHub displays nicely,
as follows:

```yaml
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
  gfm: default
```

With two formats, the `Preview` button only renders the first one.
To render both formats, run `quarto render`.
You'll try this out in the [week 15 exercises](/week15/w15_exercises.qmd#exercise-8-output-for-github).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### More YAML syntax _(Click to expand)_

- In YAML, strings usually don't need quotes,
  but they do when they contain special characters like `:` or `#`.
  For example, the title in the example above, `"Week 14: Quarto"`,
  needs quotes because of the colon.
  To be safe, you can simply always quote strings.

- Some keys take a **list of values,** which can be written in two ways:

  ```yaml
  # Block syntax: each item on a new line, preceded by a dash and a space
  author:
    - Jane Doe
    - John Smith

  # Inline syntax: comma-separated values inside square brackets
  keywords: [RNA-seq, mosquito, Plasmodium]
  ```

- As in R and the shell, a `#` starts a **comment**.
:::

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 1: YAML header

1. Change the YAML header of your `week14a.qmd` to include a title, a subtitle,
   your name as the author, today's date,
   a table of contents, and the `darkly` theme. Render the document.

<!----
   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   For example:

   ```yaml
   ---
   title: "Week 14: Quarto"
   subtitle: "Beyond the basics"
   author: "Jane Doe"
   date: 2026-11-23
   format:
     html:
       toc: true
       theme: darkly
   ---
   ```

   </details>
---->

2. Predict what will happen in each of the following cases,
   then try them one by one (and undo each change afterwards):
   - You remove the space after the colon in `toc: true`.
   - You change your title to one with a colon, like `Week 14: Quarto`, without quotes.
   - You indent `toc: true` by two spaces instead of four.

<!----
   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   In all three cases, the document won't render,
   and Quarto shows an error message about the YAML header,
   with the line number near the problem.
   In the last case, `toc` is no longer an option of the `html` format:
   Quarto now reads it as an option of `format`, which isn't valid.

   </details>
---->
:::

## R code in Quarto documents

### Running chunks

Besides `Run Cell`, which runs the current chunk,
the line above each chunk has a `Run Above` button,
which runs all code chunks _above_ the current chunk.
This is useful when you've restarted R or opened a document in a new session,
and want to get back to where you were.

<!---- TODO: Add a Positron screenshot of the Run Cell / Run Above buttons above a chunk ---->

### Chunk options

You can change how a chunk behaves with **chunk options**:
lines at the top of a chunk that start with `#|`,
where each `#|` line sets one option.
For example, this chunk would be shown in the rendered document, but not run:

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
#| eval: false
install.packages("tidyverse")
```

A few useful chunk options (more in the [Quarto documentation {{< fa external-link >}}](https://quarto.org/docs/computations/execution-options.html){target="_blank"}):

- `#| eval: false` --- Show the code but don't run it.
- `#| echo: false` --- Run the code and show its output, but hide the code itself.
  This is useful if you want to show a figure but not the code used to create it.
- `#| include: false` --- Run the code, but show neither the code nor its output.
- `#| warning: false` and `#| message: false` --- Hide warnings and messages,
  such as the ones printed when loading some packages.

Chunk options override the document-wide defaults set under `execute:` in the YAML header.
For example, if the YAML has `echo: false`,
you can still show the code of one specific chunk by adding `#| echo: true` to it.

### Figure options

When you render a document, any plots made in code chunks are included in the output.
Several chunk options control how plots are shown --- for example:

- `fig-cap` --- Add a figure caption below the plot.
- `fig-width` and `fig-height` --- Set the size of the plot (in inches).
- `out-width` --- Set the size of the plot _as shown in the document_,
  e.g. `"50%"` for half the page width.

Before we can make a plot,
we need to load the _tidyverse_ and read the gene count table from week 13:

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(tidyverse)
counts <- read_tsv(
  "/fs/ess/PAS3493/share/week13/salmon.merged.gene_counts_length_scaled.tsv"
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
counts <- read_tsv(
  "../assets/week13/salmon.merged.gene_counts_length_scaled.tsv"
)
```

Then, add a chunk with a scatter plot that compares the gene counts of two samples:

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
#| fig-cap: "Gene counts in samples S63 and S64"
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-width: "70%"
counts |>
  ggplot(aes(x = S63, y = S64)) +
  geom_point()
```

<details class="details-quiz">
<summary>What do you think will happen if you double `fig-width` and `fig-height`, but keep `out-width` the same?</summary>

_The answer will be added after class._

<!----
The plot is shown at the same size, but the text and points look much smaller ---
see the plot and explanation below.
---->

</details>

Change `fig-width` and `fig-height` to twice their size, and render again:

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
#| fig-cap: "Gene counts in samples S63 and S64"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
#| out-width: "70%"
counts |>
  ggplot(aes(x = S63, y = S64)) +
  geom_point()
```

The plot is shown at the same size as before,
but the text and points now look much smaller.
That's because of the difference between `fig-width` and `out-width`:

- `fig-width` and `fig-height` set the size of the "canvas" that R draws the plot on.
  The size of the text and points is fixed,
  so on a larger canvas, they look **smaller** (!).
  This behavior is the same as when you
  [save a plot to a file with `ggsave()`](/week13/w13b_data-viz.qmd#exporting-plots-to-files).
- `out-width` simply makes the finished plot bigger or smaller in the document.

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 2: Chunk options

1. Render your document, and note the messages printed by the chunk
   that loads the _tidyverse_ and reads the count table.
   Then, use a chunk option to **hide these messages**, and render again.

<!----
   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ````{.markdown}
   ```{{r}}
   #| message: false
   library(tidyverse)
   counts <- read_tsv(
     "/fs/ess/PAS3493/share/week13/salmon.merged.gene_counts_length_scaled.tsv"
   )
   ```
   ````

   </details>
---->

2. How would you hide the messages of _all_ chunks in a document,
   _except_ those of one chunk?

<!----
   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   Set `message: false` under `execute:` in the YAML header,
   and add `#| message: true` to the one chunk whose messages you want to show.

   </details>
---->

3. In the chunk with the scatter plot, hide the code.
   Then, make the text and points look _larger_ than in the very first version of the plot,
   **without** changing `out-width`.
   Which option(s) do you change, and how?

<!----
   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   Make `fig-width` and `fig-height` _smaller_ (keeping their ratio), for example:

   ````{.markdown}
   ```{{r}}
   #| echo: false
   #| fig-cap: "Gene counts in samples S63 and S64"
   #| fig-width: 3
   #| fig-height: 2.4
   #| out-width: "70%"
   counts |>
     ggplot(aes(x = S63, y = S64)) +
     geom_point()
   ```
   ````

   On this smaller canvas, the text and points take up a larger part of the plot,
   while `out-width` still shows the plot at the same size in the document.

   </details>
---->
:::

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 3: Let Claude render and fix your document

1. Move one of your scatter plot chunks to the top of your document,
   right below the YAML header.
   Predict: will this chunk still run when you click `Run Cell`?
   And will the document still render?
   Try both to check.

<!----
   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   The chunk still runs with `Run Cell`,
   because the _tidyverse_ is already loaded and `counts` already exists in your R session.
   But the document doesn't render,
   with the error `could not find function "ggplot"`.
   When rendering, your code runs in a new R session, from top to bottom,
   so the plot chunk now runs before the chunk that loads the _tidyverse_ and reads `counts`.

   </details>
---->

2. In Claude, ask it to render your document with `quarto render`, and to fix any errors.
   Only approve the commands that you understand.
   Which command did Claude run, and how did it fix the error?

<!----
   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   Claude runs the same `quarto render week14a.qmd` command that you saw above,
   reads the error message,
   and then either moves the plot chunk back below the chunk that loads the _tidyverse_,
   or adds the `library()` and `read_tsv()` lines to the plot chunk.
   It will then likely render the document again, to check that its fix worked.

   </details>
---->

3. Is Claude's fix the one you would have chosen?

<!----
   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   Moving the plot chunk back is the best fix.
   Adding the `library()` and `read_tsv()` lines to the plot chunk also works,
   but then your document loads the package and reads the file twice.
   As you'll see [below](#load-packages-at-the-top),
   it's best to load all packages, and define your file paths, at the top of your document.

   </details>
---->
:::

### Inline code in Markdown text

You can include the output of R code directly in your Markdown text with **inline code**:
a backtick, the letter `r` and a space, your code, and a closing backtick.
For example, this text:

```markdown
The gene count table contains `r "\x60r nrow(counts)\x60"` genes.
```

Renders as:

> The gene count table contains `r nrow(counts)` genes.

This way, numbers in your text are computed when you render the document,
so they always match your data and code --- no more copy-pasting numbers.

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Self-study exercise: Inline code

1. Add a sentence to your document that reports, with inline code,
   the number of genes with a count of zero in sample `S63`, and render.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   For example:

   ```markdown
   In sample S63, `r "\x60r nrow(filter(counts, S63 == 0))\x60"` genes have a count of zero.
   ```

   </details>

2. What will the rendered document show if you leave out the `r` and the space,
   i.e. `` `nrow(counts)` ``? Predict, then render to check.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   Without the `r`, it is regular Markdown inline code formatting:
   the text `nrow(counts)` is shown in a code font, and the code is not run.

   </details>
:::

## Structuring your Quarto document

### Load packages at the top

Load all packages that your document uses in a chunk at the top of the document.
That way, you (and others) can see at a glance which packages are needed.
For example:

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(tidyverse)
library(here)    # You'll learn about this package below
```

Install packages in the console, though, rather than in a chunk.
Otherwise, they will be installed again every time you render the document.

### State file paths at the top

As with the variables in your
[FastQC shell script in week 7](/week07/w7a_scripts1.qmd#using-variables-in-your-fastqc-script),
it's good practice to define all file paths in one place:
in a chunk near the top of your document, first for the input files,
and then for the output files.
For example:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Input files
metadata_file <- "../garrigos/meta/metadata.tsv"

# Output files
outdir <- "results"
plot_file <- "results/boxplot.png"
```

In the rest of the document, you then only use these variables,
like `read_tsv(metadata_file)`, `dir.create(outdir, showWarnings = FALSE)`,
and `ggsave(filename = plot_file, ...)`.
This has two advantages:

- You (and others) can see at a glance which files the document reads and writes.
- When a path changes, you only need to change it in one place.

### The working directory when rendering, and the `here` package

When you render, your code runs in a new R session,
and that session's working directory can differ from that of your Console:

- When you **run code interactively**, the working dir is the **folder you opened**.
- When you **render**, the working dir is the folder **that contains the document**.

So far, your Quarto documents have been directly inside the folder you opened,
so these two working directories were the same.
But in larger projects,
where you'll want to keep your **Quarto documents in a subfolder**,
like `scripts`, they will differ,
and a relative path may work in one case but not the other.

The [_here_ package {{< fa external-link >}}](https://here.r-lib.org/){target="_blank"} solves this problem:
its `here()` function creates absolute file paths from relative ones that start
at your **project's top-level folder**, no matter what your working directory is.
(It finds that folder by looking for a `.git` folder^[
  Or an empty placeholder file called `.here`.]
in your working dir and its parent folders.)

For example, say that your final project's Git repository `FP` is open in Positron,
and a Quarto document `FP/scripts/analysis.qmd` reads the file `FP/data/meta.tsv`:

|                   | Working dir  | `read_tsv("data/meta.tsv")` | `read_tsv(here("data/meta.tsv"))` |
| ----------------- | ------------ | :-------------------------: | :-------------------------------: |
| **Run interactively** | `FP`     | [{{< fa check title="Works" >}}]{.text-success} | [{{< fa check title="Works" >}}]{.text-success} |
| **Render**            | `FP/scripts` | [{{< fa xmark title="Fails" >}}]{.text-danger} | [{{< fa check title="Works" >}}]{.text-success} |

: {.striped .hover}

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
To use `here()`, install it with `install.packages("here")`,
and load it with `library(here)`.
You'll try this out in the [week 15 exercises](/week15/w15_exercises.qmd#exercise-7-rendering-from-a-subfolder).
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
#### Why not use `setwd()`? _(Click to expand)_

You may come across code that solves this problem with `setwd()`,
which changes the working directory.
Avoid it: `setwd()` usually needs the full path to your project folder,
so the code breaks as soon as the project is moved or someone else runs it.
:::

### Record R and package versions at the end

For reproducibility, it's good practice to record which versions of R and R packages you used.
An easy way to do so is to end each Quarto document with a chunk that runs `sessionInfo()`.
Its output lists your R version, your operating system,
and the versions of all loaded packages.
Here is the output from when I rendered this page on my laptop
(on OSC, yours will show Linux and different versions):

```{r}
sessionInfo()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Project-specific packages with **renv** _(Click to expand)_

By default, all your projects share one set of installed packages,
so updating a package for one project also changes it for all others.
This isn't great for reproducibility.
Moreover, reinstalling the exact versions from a `sessionInfo()` list,
say on another computer, is tedious.

The **renv** package solves both problems:
it gives each project its own packages,
and records their versions in a file that lets you (or anyone else)
reinstall those exact versions with a single command ---
see the [optional self-study page on renv](/bonus/renv.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Use an R _script_ for long-running code _(Click to expand)_

Quarto documents are best kept quick to render, ideally within a couple of minutes.
If your analysis includes slow steps, such as a large differential expression analysis,
the recommended strategy is to put them in separate R scripts,
which you can run in a Slurm batch job.
See the [optional self-study page on R](/bonus/r.qmd#running-r-in-a-slurm-batch-job)
for how to do this.
:::

## Recap and self-study

### Recap

- Rendering first runs all code, and then converts the result to the output format;
  `quarto render` renders a document from the terminal.
- The YAML header sets document metadata, output format options,
  and, under `execute:`, default options for all chunks.
- Chunk options (`#|` lines) control whether a chunk's code is run and shown,
  and how its figures are shown.
- Inline code puts R output directly in your Markdown text.
- Load packages and define file paths at the top of a document,
  and end it with `sessionInfo()`.
- When rendering, the working directory is the document's folder;
  `here()` makes file paths work both interactively and when rendering.

### Optional self-study material

The [optional Quarto self-study page](/bonus/quarto.qmd) covers:

- Naming chunks with chunk labels
- Two Positron features for Quarto documents:
  showing the output below each chunk, and the visual editor
- Citing papers and software with a bibliography file
- Avoiding slow re-renders with caching
- Turning an existing R script into a Quarto document
- Using Claude with Quarto: slide decks, citations, and websites
